## MAC-015 — Compact source map  
**Source:** OECD Economic Surveys: Mexico 2022, pp. 56–78  
**Type/role:** Policy synthesis; international organization. **No score.**

### Atomic claims

- **Observed/reported fact — targeting:** The share of households in the three lowest income deciles receiving monetary transfers has fallen, while for the rest of deciles it has increased; the comparison uses federal cash programmes captured in the **2018 and 2021 ENIGH survey waves**, whose programme sets differ. **Locator:** pp. 54–56, opening paragraph and Figure 1.36 note. **Use:** 5B.8–9.

- **Modelled scenario, not outcome:** Simulations using Mexico's 2020 ENIGH household data suggest that introducing a 3-month unemployment benefit complemented with 3-month income support for informal workers who lose their job would cause poverty to fall by **11.6 percentage points (from 43.9% to 32.3%)**; results are explicitly "indicative" and assumption-dependent. **Locator:** p. 54, Box 1.10, Table 1.9 and notes (1)–(3). **Use:** 5B.8–9.

- **Modelled fiscal estimates:** OECD calculations put the illustrative fiscal cost at **−0.4% of GDP** for unemployment benefits (3 months; minimum-wage benefits), **−1%** for informal-worker income support, **−1.3%** for boosting public investment, and **−0.7%** for expanding the childcare network; illustrative revenue gains total **+3.5% of GDP**, contingent on benchmark and tax-base assumptions. **Locator:** p. 55, Table 1.10 and note. **Use:** 5B.3; recommendations, not enacted policy.

- **Reported fact + OECD interpretation:** Sembrando Vida had been deployed in **20 regions** and covered **430,000 individuals (as of 30 August 2021)**. OECD describes it as a programme that "holds promise" and calls for thorough evaluation and design revision. **Locator:** p. 55, "Boosting coverage…" ¶1. **Use:** 5B.7–9. No realized climate or social effect established in the extract.

- **Administrative fragmentation:** Federal programmes fell from **272 (2009) to 123 (2021)**; **57%** of the 123 are delivered directly and have a beneficiary register. CONEVAL counted **1,444 state** and **6,829 municipal** programmes. OECD recommends a registry covering all government levels. **Locator:** p. 56, paragraph after Figure 1.36, citing CONEVAL, 2021 [43]. **Use:** 5B.6–9.

- **Implemented reform with unresolved performance:** New specialized independent courts — the centres for labour conciliation and registration — were created, with new rules for union representation and collective bargaining (personal, free, direct and secret vote). The target is resolution of at least **60%** of worker–company conflicts through conciliation; when conciliation fails, oral trials should allow resolution in under **6 months**. OECD says full implementation throughout the country, including at state level, will be key. **Locator:** pp. 57–58, "Key reforms…" ¶1. **Use:** 5B.4, 5B.6. Targets are not observed results.

- **Reported labour outcomes, attribution unresolved:** Minimum wages rose **50% in real terms from 2019 to 2021**; **around 13% of full-time workers** earn the minimum wage (Conasami, 2021 [44]). Previous evaluations suggest past increases did not harm employment in the lower part of the distribution (Conasami, 2019 [45]); OECD says further evaluations of recent increases are warranted and warns about formal-employment risks. **Locator:** p. 58, ¶2. **Use:** 5B.4, 5B.7–8.

- **Administrative claim:** A reform to reduce fraud in the use of outsourcing was approved in **April 2021**, agreed with the private sector after its reformulation. Before the reform, **around 20% of formal workers** were subcontracted under an outsourcing scheme; after the reform, subcontracting is only allowed for specialized services not part of the firm's main activity, and subcontracting firms must be officially registered with the Labour Ministry. Based on administrative data, **around 2.7 million workers have migrated to standard contracts so far** and **the salary has increased around 12% on average**. OECD also flags a potential formal-job-creation risk. **Locator:** p. 58, final paragraph. **Use:** 5B.4, 5B.8. Extract does not establish causality, comparison population, or data source details.

- **Government projection, not realized outcome:** Starting in **2023**, employer's pension contributions will increase gradually over **8 years, 1% per year, from 5.5% to 13.87%**; the number of minimum years to access pensions has been lowered from **25 to 15 years** and will gradually reach **around 19 years by 2030**. **Government estimates** suggest the reform will expand access, reaching **80% of formal workers** once fully implemented. OECD projects pension spending to rise from **4% of GDP** currently to **5.3% of GDP in 2026**, increasing budget rigidity. **Locator:** p. 59, ¶¶1–2. **Use:** 5B.3, 5B.8–10.

- **Observed access gap:** The share of the population reporting lack of access to health services increased **from 16% in 2018 to 28% in 2020 (Coneval, 2021 [38])**, even though they are entitled to coverage by INSABI; OECD reads this as evidence that achieving truly universal coverage remains a challenge. **Locator:** p. 59, ¶4. **Use:** 5B.6, 5B.8–9.

- **Distributional facts:** Female labour-force participation continues to lag the OECD average and other Latin American countries; **Mexican women suffer from a 10% pay gap** (p. 59). The recently replaced network of free childcare facilities (Estancias Infantiles) was substituted by subsidies deemed insufficient, and the number of recipients was reduced; **achieving full coverage for children under 6 would cost 1.2% of GDP annually**, versus existing spending of **0.5% of GDP** (UN and ECLAC, 2020 [42]). OECD recommends prioritizing low-income households and ensuring access is not linked to labour-market status so informal workers also get access. **Locator:** pp. 59–60. **Use:** 5B.6, 5B.8.

- **Education shock:** **3 million Mexicans at primary and secondary education level interrupted their studies and did not restart the 2020–2021 academic year (INEGI, 2021 [51])**. OECD describes long-term effects as likely, not observed, and recommends reintegration, tutoring, and monitoring. **Locator:** pp. 61–62, paragraphs surrounding Figures 1.40–1.41. **Use:** 5B.6, 5B.9–10.

- **Climate trajectory:** In **2015** Mexico committed to reducing greenhouse-gas emissions **by 22% relative to a business-as-usual scenario by 2030**, and targets have not been strengthened since then. Emissions were estimated to fall by **13% in 2020** due to the pandemic recession; under currently implemented policies this reduction will not be maintained and Mexico, like many other OECD countries, will not meet its emission targets (Climate Action Tracker, 2021 [53]). **Locator:** p. 63, ¶1. **Use:** 5B.10; forecast/assessment, not adjudicated outcome.

- **Pending legal-policy proposal:** A constitutional reform proposal of the electricity market was announced in **September 2021**; it is expected to be debated in Congress in **2022**. The proposal establishes a guaranteed market share of **at least 54%** for CFE, expands CFE's role in sector oversight, eliminates independent sector regulators, places CFE in charge of setting tariffs and granting permits, and prioritizes dispatch of electricity generated by the state-owned company. **Locator:** p. 64, Box 1.11. **Use:** 5B.2, 5B.4. Procedural status is proposal pending Congress; extract supplies no enacted text, article numbers, amendments, exceptions, or effective date.

- **Contrary material:** Regulations affecting renewable-energy projects have been subject to significant uncertainty; the Ministry of Energy has introduced several reform attempts, challenged legally by market participants and whose implementation was suspended by courts. The Ministry cited **oversupply of renewables permits exceeding grid capacity, geographical unbalances, intermittency**, and (Box 1.11) energy security to favour conventional-based generation; OECD counters with IEA evidence that renewables can lower energy costs, provide flexibility, and reduce blackout risk (IEA, 2019 [57]). **Locator:** p. 64, ¶¶1–3 and Box 1.11. **Use:** 5B.4, 5B.6, 5B.10. Litigation outcomes and cited legal authorities are absent from the extract.

- **OECD synthesis/recommendations:** The chapter characterizes weak competition, reform reversals and planned regulatory changes in electricity and oil markets as increasing investor uncertainty, **about 55% worker informality**, lagging anticorruption implementation, limited countercyclical capacity (the existing current-spending rule covers around 36% of public-sector expenditure), and **support to PEMEX of 1% of GDP** as material weaknesses. Recommendations include an independent fiscal council and a long-term debt anchor; preserving central-bank autonomy; strengthening competition, procurement transparency, and the anticorruption toolkit; and a comprehensive strategy to reduce the cost of formalization. **Locator:** pp. 67–68, Table 1.13. **Use:** 5B.2–7. These are OECD assessments, not proof of implementation or AMLO-specific causation.

- **Chapter 2 framing (pp. 75–76):** Access to formal financial services in Mexico is particularly low and unequal across income, gender, rural/urban areas, and states; **around one-eighth of municipalities** lack any financial access point; while **around 98% of the population has access to one financial point**, shares fall to **81% in Oaxaca, 93% in Chiapas, and 94% in Yucatan**. **Locator:** pp. 75–76. **Use:** cross-chapter context only; extract does not provide source years, denominators, or causal analysis behind these disparities.

### Limitations and reopen list

The extract blends OECD interpretation, secondary statistics, simulations, government estimates, and recommendations; most claims concern Mexico's institutions/economy rather than decisions attributable personally to AMLO. Reopen: Figure 1.37's obscured labels; underlying administrative data for outsourcing reform; pension legislation text, enactment status, and full implementation schedule; electricity/oil reform texts, amendments, court dockets and final status; methodology behind the health-access and programme-coverage changes; fiscal-table assumptions and benchmark years; and Chapter 2's financial-access statistics — the pp. 77–78 material is largely synthesis/correlation and lacks source years, denominators, causal limits, and state-level datasets beyond the Oaxaca/Chiapas/Yucatan access-point figures cited above.
